title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context: §§36–43 of E555 interpolate a curve through equally spaced points by means of a 'finite equation', i.e. a partial-fraction (cotangent-type) series. In the sine example (data lying on y = sin x) the method gives y at abscissa ωπ only in terms of a quantity Δ defined by Beta-type integrals. To show that the interpolant really is sin ωπ, one needs
(1-2n) ∫_0^1 z^{ω-n}(1-z)^{-n-ω} dz · ∫_0^1 z^{n+ω-1}(1-z)^{n-ω} dz = (n-ω)π sin nπ cos nπ / (n sin(n-ω)π sin(n+ω)π).
This is the Theorem of §44, begun on p.197 and proved on this page.

Proof on p.198–199, in modern terms:
1. Put n+ω = μ/λ and ω-n = ν/λ, so 2n = (μ-ν)/λ and 1-2n = (λ-μ+ν)/λ.
2. Substitute z = v^λ. Each substitution contributes a factor λ, so the left side becomes λ(λ-μ+ν)·(λ+ν | λ-μ)·(μ | λ-ν).
3. Here Euler's symbol (p|q) = ∫_0^1 v^{p-1}(1-v^λ)^{q/λ-1} dv = (1/λ)B(p/λ, q/λ). This is symmetric in p and q.
4. Apply the recursion (p|q) = (p-λ)/(p+q-λ)·(p-λ|q). This turns the left side into λν (λ-μ|ν)(λ-ν|μ).
5. Use the reflection-type evaluation (λ-q|p)(λ+p-q|q) = π/(λ p sin(qπ/λ)) with p = μ-ν, q = μ. Combine it with (λ-ν|ν) = π/(λ sin νπ/λ).
6. Use the exchange identity (p|q)(p+q|r) = (p|r)(p+r|q) with p = λ-μ, q = μ-ν, r = ν. Together with (λ-μ+ν|μ-ν) = π/(λ sin((μ-ν)π/λ)), this gives
λν (λ-μ|ν)(λ-ν|μ) = (ν/(μ-ν))·π sin((μ-ν)π/λ)/(sin(μπ/λ) sin(νπ/λ)).
7. The right side of the theorem transforms into exactly this, which proves the theorem.

Modern content: with a = μ/λ and b = ν/λ,
B(1-a,b)B(1-b,a) = Γ(a)Γ(1-a)Γ(b)Γ(1-b)/(Γ(1+a-b)Γ(1-a+b)) = π sin π(a-b) / ((a-b) sin πa sin πb).
This is an immediate consequence of Γ(x)Γ(1-x) = π/sin πx.

Corollary 1 (§45) records that this product of two such integrals is expressible 'per solos angulos'.
errors: The second integral as transcribed has exponent z^{(μ-ν-λ)/λ}, i.e. v^{μ-ν-1} after substitution. From the theorem (z^{n+ω-1} with n+ω = μ/λ) it must be z^{(μ-λ)/λ}, i.e. v^{μ-1}. The bracket (μ|λ-ν) that Euler actually uses is correct. So any stray '-ν' is either a transcription error or a misprint, and it is harmless to the argument.
No mathematical errors otherwise. I verified every reduction (recursion, reflection product, exchange identity) and the final trigonometric matching.

ideas.what: Product of two Euler integrals (p|q) evaluated purely in terms of sines, proving that the interpolated curve is the sine curve.
ideas.modern_name: Consequence of the reflection formula Γ(x)Γ(1-x)=π/sin πx applied to B(1-a,b)B(1-b,a)
ideas.where_published: E321 'Observationes circa integralia formularum ∫x^{p-1}dx(1-x^n)^{q/n-1}' and related Euler papers on such integrals; E555 itself.
E321 (Novi Comm. Petrop. 1766/67) and related papers

ideas.what: Using an integral identity to certify that a partial-fraction interpolation through the sample points sin(kπ±nπ) reproduces sin ωπ for all ω, not just at the nodes.
ideas.modern_name: Uniqueness/correctness check of cardinal-type (cotangent series) interpolation

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a correct, routine application of Euler's well-known (p|q) Beta-integral calculus (reflection and exchange identities from E321). It serves to confirm the sine interpolation example. Nothing here appears new or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: Second integral in the first displayed equation should read ∫ z^{(μ-λ)/λ} dz / (1-z)^{ν/λ}, i.e. z^{n+ω-1}. The '-ν' in the exponent appears spurious; check against the image.
After the substitution z=v^λ, the second integral should be ∫ v^{μ-1} dv / (1-v^λ)^{ν/λ}, not v^{μ-ν-1}.
In Corollary 1 the integrand is v^{p-1}dv / (1-v^λ)^{(λ-q)/λ}, i.e. the λ-th root of (1-v^λ)^{λ-q}.
